demos.description: A ten-part, self-contained verification of every exact result in the theory on explicit finite data. It checks by brute force that the transitive dependency closure is the least dependency-closed superset of a base set; confirms the inclusion-exclusion merge identity as an integer equality; enumerates all self-contained developments covering a three-statement corpus and confirms that the canonical library embeds in every one of them and maximises fitness; exhibits the two-route failure of canonicity together with a branch-free minimum-cost cover; verifies the exact k-fold reuse identity and the resulting strict fitness dominance; tabulates the composition phase transition across its threshold, asserting the trichotomy at each adapter value; enumerates dependency-closed subsets to confirm the counts 2^n, n+1 and exact multiplicativity across an independent split; computes the guaranteed and realised relative overshoot of an adapter valley together with a table of overshoots against the two efficiency exponents; locates all three strict local maxima of a nine-development landscape and identifies which are global; and drives raw theorem-per-line fitness above prescribed targets by conservative inflation while confirming the semantics never changes. Every claim is guarded by an assertion; the script uses exact rational arithmetic throughout and the standard library only.
demos.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Dependency-Adjusted Fitness of Mathematical Theories
====================================================

Numerical demonstrations of the exact results in the accompanying paper.

A *theory* is recorded by the transitive dependency closure of the material it
uses, together with the corpus statements it proves.  Its dependency-adjusted
cost is the total source length of that closure, each item charged exactly
once; its fitness is (statements proved) / cost.

The demonstrations below verify, on explicit finite data:

  1. Canonicity of the transitive closure: it is the LEAST dependency-closed
     superset of a base set.
  2. Exact merge accounting:  cost(T u U) + shared mass = cost(T) + cost(U).
  3. Fitness is the ordinal inverse of cost on a fixed corpus; the canonical
     library (the closure of the corpus' proof bases) is the global champion.
  4. Failure of canonicity with two inequivalent proof routes -- two cost-equal
     champions whose closures have empty intersection -- and survival of a
     minimum-cost cover.
  5. The exact k-fold reuse identity:
        cost(library) + k * core = sum_i cost(specialist_i) + core.
  6. The composition phase transition: fitness rises / is neutral / falls
     according as adapter cost < / = / > shared dependency mass.
  7. Exact candidate counts: independent parts multiply, the free family of n
     items has 2^n usable sub-libraries, the chain has exactly n+1.
  8. The quantitative adapter valley: guaranteed relative overshoot
     (alpha - beta) / (1 + beta).
  9. Three-style metastability: three distinct strict local maxima, only one
     of which is global.
 10. No global maximum without normalisation: raw theorems-per-line diverges
     under conservative inflation, while the semantics never changes.

Pure standard library; run with `python3 demo.py`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import chain, combinations
from math import isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, Iterator, List, Optional, Set, Tuple

Item = int
Deps = Dict[Item, Set[Item]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Core machinery
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_dependency_closed(deps: Deps, s: Iterable[Item]) -> bool:
    """A set is dependency-closed when it contains the direct dependencies of
    each of its members -- i.e. it is a self-contained development."""
    sset = set(s)
    return all(deps.get(i, set()) <= sset for i in sset)


def transitive_closure(deps: Deps, base: Iterable[Item]) -> Set[Item]:
    """The least dependency-closed superset of `base`.

    Worklist expansion; terminates in at most |universe| rounds.
    """
    out: Set[Item] = set(base)
    work: List[Item] = list(out)
    while work:
        i = work.pop()
        for j in deps.get(i, set()):
            if j not in out:
                out.add(j)
                work.append(j)
    return out


def cost(length: Callable[[Item], int], closure: Iterable[Item]) -> int:
    """Dependency-adjusted cost: each item in the closure charged once."""
    return sum(length(i) for i in closure)


def fitness(n_proved: int, c: int) -> Fraction:
    """Corpus statements proved per unit of dependency-adjusted cost."""
    return Fraction(n_proved, c)


def powerset(items: Iterable[Item]) -> Iterator[Tuple[Item, ...]]:
    xs = list(items)
    return chain.from_iterable(combinations(xs, r) for r in range(len(xs) + 1))


def closed_subsets(deps: Deps, universe: Iterable[Item]) -> List[FrozenSet[Item]]:
    """All usable sub-libraries: dependency-closed subsets of the universe."""
    us = list(universe)
    return [
        frozenset(s) for s in powerset(us) if is_dependency_closed(deps, s)
    ]


def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Canonicity of the transitive closure
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_closure_minimality() -> None:
    banner("1.  The transitive closure is the LEAST dependency-closed superset")

    # 0 <- 1 <- 2,  3 <- 4,  5 isolated
    deps: Deps = {0: set(), 1: {0}, 2: {1}, 3: set(), 4: {3}, 5: set()}
    universe = set(deps)
    base = {2, 4}

    cl = transitive_closure(deps, base)
    print(f"  dependency structure : {{i: deps(i)}} = "
          f"{{ {', '.join(f'{k}:{sorted(v)}' for k, v in deps.items())} }}")
    print(f"  base                 : {sorted(base)}")
    print(f"  transitive closure   : {sorted(cl)}")
    print(f"  is dependency-closed : {is_dependency_closed(deps, cl)}")

    # Check minimality by brute force over every dependency-closed superset.
    supersets = [
        s for s in closed_subsets(deps, universe) if base <= set(s)
    ]
    minimal = all(cl <= set(s) for s in supersets)
    print(f"  dependency-closed supersets of the base : {len(supersets)}")
    print(f"  closure contained in every one of them  : {minimal}")
    assert minimal and is_dependency_closed(deps, cl)
    print("  => the cost model is canonical: no accounting slack.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Exact merge accounting (inclusion-exclusion)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_merge_accounting() -> None:
    banner("2.  Exact merge accounting:  cost(T u U) + shared = cost(T) + cost(U)")

    length = lambda i: 10 * (i + 1)
    ct = {0, 1, 2, 3}
    cu = {2, 3, 4, 5}

    merged = ct | cu
    shared = ct & cu
    lhs = cost(length, merged) + cost(length, shared)
    rhs = cost(length, ct) + cost(length, cu)

    print(f"  closure(T) = {sorted(ct)}   cost = {cost(length, ct)}")
    print(f"  closure(U) = {sorted(cu)}   cost = {cost(length, cu)}")
    print(f"  pooled     = {sorted(merged)}   cost = {cost(length, merged)}")
    print(f"  shared     = {sorted(shared)}   mass = {cost(length, shared)}")
    print(f"  {cost(length, merged)} + {cost(length, shared)} = {lhs}"
          f"   vs   {cost(length, ct)} + {cost(length, cu)} = {rhs}")
    assert lhs == rhs
    print("  => pooling saves EXACTLY the shared mass.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The canonical library is the global champion
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_canonical_champion() -> None:
    banner("3.  The canonical library is the dependency-adjusted global champion")

    # Items 0..7.  Corpus statements have proof bases inside the items.
    deps: Deps = {0: set(), 1: {0}, 2: {1}, 3: {0}, 4: {3}, 5: set(), 6: {5}, 7: {6}}
    length = lambda i: 5
    corpus_bases = {"s1": {2}, "s2": {4}}          # two statements, one route each
    universe = set(deps)

    base = set().union(*corpus_bases.values())
    canonical = transitive_closure(deps, base)
    can_cost = cost(length, canonical)
    print(f"  proof bases    : {corpus_bases}")
    print(f"  canonical lib  : {sorted(canonical)}  cost = {can_cost}"
          f"  fitness = {fitness(2, can_cost)}")

    # Every dependency-closed competitor that covers the corpus.
    competitors = [
        s for s in closed_subsets(deps, universe)
        if all(b <= set(s) for b in corpus_bases.values())
    ]
    print(f"  dependency-closed covering developments : {len(competitors)}")
    worst = max(competitors, key=lambda s: cost(length, s))
    print(f"  most bloated competitor : {sorted(worst)}"
          f"  fitness = {fitness(2, cost(length, worst))}")
    ok = all(
        fitness(2, cost(length, s)) <= fitness(2, can_cost) for s in competitors
    )
    embeds = all(canonical <= set(s) for s in competitors)
    print(f"  canonical closure embeds in every competitor : {embeds}")
    print(f"  canonical library has maximal fitness        : {ok}")
    assert ok and embeds
    print("  => reuse wins structurally: every rival must contain the shared core.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Two routes destroy canonicity, but not existence
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def min_cost_cover(
    length: Callable[[Item], int],
    routes: Dict[str, List[Set[Item]]],
    universe: Set[Item],
) -> Tuple[FrozenSet[Item], int]:
    """Minimum-cost covering sub-library under alternative proof routes.

    Exhaustive over subsets of the universe: exponential, and provably so in
    general (the problem is a weighted set cover in disguise).
    """
    best: Optional[FrozenSet[Item]] = None
    best_cost = None
    for s in powerset(sorted(universe)):
        sset = set(s)
        if all(any(r <= sset for r in rs) for rs in routes.values()):
            c = cost(length, sset)
            if best_cost is None or c < best_cost:
                best, best_cost = frozenset(sset), c
    assert best is not None and best_cost is not None
    return best, best_cost


def demo_two_routes() -> None:
    banner("4.  Two inequivalent proof routes: canonicity fails, existence survives")

    length = lambda i: 1
    r1, r2 = {1}, {2}
    print(f"  one statement, two routes: {sorted(r1)} and {sorted(r2)}")
    f1, f2 = fitness(1, cost(length, r1)), fitness(1, cost(length, r2))
    print(f"  fitness of route 1 = {f1},  fitness of route 2 = {f2}  (equal)")
    print(f"  closures incomparable : {not (r1 <= r2) and not (r2 <= r1)}")
    print(f"  intersection          : {sorted(r1 & r2)}  (proves nothing)")
    assert f1 == f2 and not (r1 <= r2) and not (r2 <= r1) and not (r1 & r2)
    print("  => no least covering closure exists; the champion is only")
    print("     determined up to cost.")

    print()
    print("  But a minimum-cost cover is still attained.  A larger instance:")
    routes = {
        "s1": [{1, 2}, {3}],
        "s2": [{2, 4}, {3, 4}],
        "s3": [{5}, {1, 3}],
    }
    lengths = {1: 4, 2: 4, 3: 5, 4: 2, 5: 9}
    length2 = lambda i: lengths[i]
    cover, c = min_cost_cover(length2, routes, set(lengths))
    print(f"  routes  : {routes}")
    print(f"  lengths : {lengths}")
    print(f"  minimum-cost cover : {sorted(cover)}  cost = {c}"
          f"  fitness = {fitness(3, c)}")
    print("  => existence is robust; only the METHOD of finding the optimum")
    print("     changes, from a closure computation to a set-cover search.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Exact k-fold reuse identity
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_reuse_identity() -> None:
    banner("5.  Exact k-fold reuse identity: specialists waste (k-1) copies of the core")

    length = lambda i: 3
    core = {100, 101, 102, 103}
    privs = {0: {0, 1}, 1: {2, 3, 4}, 2: {5}, 3: {6, 7}}
    k = len(privs)

    library = core | set().union(*privs.values())
    lib_cost = cost(length, library)
    spec_costs = {i: cost(length, core | p) for i, p in privs.items()}
    core_cost = cost(length, core)

    lhs = lib_cost + k * core_cost
    rhs = sum(spec_costs.values()) + core_cost

    print(f"  core          : {sorted(core)}   cost = {core_cost}")
    for i, p in privs.items():
        print(f"  specialist {i}  : core + {sorted(p)}   cost = {spec_costs[i]}")
    print(f"  shared library: cost = {lib_cost}")
    print(f"  identity      : {lib_cost} + {k}*{core_cost} = {lhs}"
          f"   vs   {sum(spec_costs.values())} + {core_cost} = {rhs}")
    assert lhs == rhs
    print(f"  waste of the suite = (k-1)*core = {(k - 1) * core_cost}")

    corpus = 12
    print(f"  fitness, suite   = {fitness(corpus, sum(spec_costs.values()))}")
    print(f"  fitness, library = {fitness(corpus, lib_cost)}   (strictly greater)")
    assert fitness(corpus, lib_cost) > fitness(corpus, sum(spec_costs.values()))
    print("  => the saving grows LINEARLY in the number of clients.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  The composition phase transition
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_phase_transition() -> None:
    banner("6.  Composition phase transition at adapter = shared mass")

    length = lambda i: 10
    ct, cu = {0, 1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4, 5}
    n_corpus = 4

    shared = cost(length, ct & cu)
    dup = cost(length, ct) + cost(length, cu)
    pooled = cost(length, ct | cu)

    print(f"  duplicate cost = {dup},  pooled cost = {pooled},"
          f"  shared mass = {shared}")
    print(f"  dependency density rho = {Fraction(shared, dup)}")
    print()
    print("     A   composed cost   composed fitness   duplicated fitness   verdict")
    print("   " + "-" * 70)
    for a in (0, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40):
        comp = pooled + a
        fc, fd = fitness(n_corpus, comp), fitness(n_corpus, dup)
        verdict = "GAIN " if fc > fd else ("neutral" if fc == fd else "LOSS ")
        # the trichotomy, verified numerically
        assert (fc > fd) == (a < shared)
        assert (fc == fd) == (a == shared)
        assert (fc < fd) == (a > shared)
        print(f"   {a:3d}   {comp:12d}   {str(fc):>16}   {str(fd):>18}   {verdict}")
    print()
    print(f"  => the crossing sits exactly at A = shared mass = {shared}.")

    print()
    print("  Product corpora: candidates multiply while costs add.")
    ct_cost, cu_cost, adapter = 100, 60, 40
    for m in (2, 3, 5, 10):
        comp = ct_cost + cu_cost + adapter          # upper bound on composed cost
        f_single = Fraction(4, ct_cost)
        f_product = Fraction(4 * m, comp)
        flag = "composition wins" if f_product > f_single else "component wins"
        print(f"   |P(U)| = {m:2d}:  single = {f_single}   product = {f_product}"
              f"   -> {flag}")
    print("  => multiplicative growth eventually beats additive cost,")
    print("     whatever the adapter charge.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7.  Exact candidate counts
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_candidate_counts() -> None:
    banner("7.  Exact counts of usable sub-libraries")

    print("   n |  free (2^n)  chain (n+1)   verified by enumeration")
    print("  " + "-" * 58)
    for n in range(1, 9):
        free_deps: Deps = {i: set() for i in range(n)}
        chain_deps: Deps = {i: (set() if i == 0 else {i - 1}) for i in range(n)}
        universe = list(range(n))
        n_free = len(closed_subsets(free_deps, universe))
        n_chain = len(closed_subsets(chain_deps, universe))
        assert n_free == 2 ** n and n_chain == n + 1
        print(f"  {n:2d} | {2 ** n:11d}  {n + 1:11d}   free={n_free}, chain={n_chain}  OK")
    print("  => for every n >= 2 the chain has strictly fewer usable")
    print("     sub-libraries, and the gap is exponential.")

    print()
    print("  Independent parts multiply exactly:")
    # A = {0,1,2} a chain; B = {10,11} free; no dependency crosses.
    deps: Deps = {0: set(), 1: {0}, 2: {1}, 10: set(), 11: set()}
    a_items, b_items = [0, 1, 2], [10, 11]
    na = len(closed_subsets(deps, a_items))
    nb = len(closed_subsets(deps, b_items))
    nab = len(closed_subsets(deps, a_items + b_items))
    print(f"   N(A) = {na}  (chain of 3)")
    print(f"   N(B) = {nb}  (free pair)")
    print(f"   N(A u B) = {nab}   and   N(A)*N(B) = {na * nb}")
    assert nab == na * nb
    print("  => a bijection, not an estimate.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8.  The quantitative adapter valley
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_adapter_valley() -> None:
    banner("8.  The quantitative adapter valley")

    content = Fraction(100)
    alpha, beta = Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(1, 10)
    # A three-state migration across an interface boundary.
    walk = [
        {"len": (1 + beta) * content, "iface": 0},   # efficient endpoint
        {"len": (1 + alpha) * content, "iface": 0},  # boundary-crossing state
        {"len": (1 + beta) * content, "iface": 1},   # efficient endpoint
    ]
    m = min(walk[0]["len"], walk[-1]["len"])
    guaranteed = (alpha - beta) / (1 + beta)

    # locate the crossing step -- it must exist since the endpoints differ
    crossing = next(
        i for i in range(len(walk) - 1) if walk[i]["iface"] != walk[i + 1]["iface"]
    )
    realised = (walk[crossing]["len"] - m) / m

    print(f"  content C = {content},  alpha = {alpha},  beta = {beta}")
    print(f"  states    : lengths {[str(w['len']) for w in walk]},"
          f" interfaces {[w['iface'] for w in walk]}")
    print(f"  crossing step index          : {crossing}")
    print(f"  smaller endpoint length m    : {m}")
    print(f"  guaranteed relative overshoot: (a-b)/(1+b) = {guaranteed}"
          f" = {float(guaranteed):.4f}")
    print(f"  realised relative overshoot  : {realised} = {float(realised):.4f}")
    assert realised >= guaranteed
    print("  => the bound is attained: the valley is unavoidable, and its depth")
    print("     depends only on the two efficiency exponents.")

    print()
    print("  Guaranteed overshoot as a function of the exponents:")
    print("     beta \\ alpha    0.25      0.50      0.75      1.00")
    for b in (Fraction(0), Fraction(1, 20), Fraction(1, 10), Fraction(1, 5)):
        row = []
        for a in (Fraction(1, 4), Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(3, 4), Fraction(1)):
            row.append(f"{float((a - b) / (1 + b)):8.4f}" if b < a else "       -")
        print(f"       {float(b):5.2f}     " + "  ".join(row))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 9.  Three-style metastability
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_metastability() -> None:
    banner("9.  Three-style metastability: three peaks, only one of them global")

    fit = [Fraction(x) for x in (1, 2, 5, 3, 7, 4, 6, 2, 9)]
    style = [i // 3 for i in range(9)]
    names = {0: "algebraic", 1: "analytic", 2: "combinatorial"}
    adj = lambda i, j: style[i] == style[j]   # bounded refactorings preserve style

    def is_strict_local_max(b: int) -> bool:
        return all(fit[t] < fit[b] for t in range(9) if adj(b, t) and t != b)

    peaks = [b for b in range(9) if is_strict_local_max(b)]
    print("  development :  " + "  ".join(f"{i}" for i in range(9)))
    print("  fitness     :  " + "  ".join(f"{int(f)}" for f in fit))
    print("  style       :  " + "  ".join(f"{s}" for s in style))
    print()
    for b in peaks:
        print(f"  strict local maximum: development {b}"
              f"  (fitness {int(fit[b])}, {names[style[b]]})")
    assert peaks == [2, 4, 8]
    assert len({style[b] for b in peaks}) == 3
    globalmax = max(range(9), key=lambda i: fit[i])
    print(f"  global maximum      : development {globalmax}"
          f"  (fitness {int(fit[globalmax])})")
    print(f"  peaks that are NOT global: "
          f"{[b for b in peaks if fit[b] < fit[globalmax]]}")
    print("  => no path of small local improvements connects the algebraic peak")
    print("     to the strictly better combinatorial one.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 10.  No global maximum without normalisation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_no_global_maximum() -> None:
    banner("10.  Raw theorems-per-line has no maximum -- and the witnesses say nothing")

    # A concrete language: a development is (count, len); stating n further
    # consequences of what is already proved costs floor(sqrt(n)) extra lines
    # and does not change the semantics.
    def extend(dev: Tuple[int, int], n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
        return (dev[0] + n, dev[1] + isqrt(n))

    def raw(dev: Tuple[int, int]) -> Fraction:
        return Fraction(dev[0], dev[1])

    base = (10, 100)
    print(f"  base development: {base[0]} statements in {base[1]} lines,"
          f"  raw fitness = {float(raw(base)):.4f}")
    print()
    print("            n     count      len   raw fitness   semantics changed?")
    print("  " + "-" * 66)
    for n in (0, 10 ** 2, 10 ** 4, 10 ** 6, 10 ** 8, 10 ** 10):
        d = extend(base, n)
        print(f"  {n:11d}   {d[0]:8d} {d[1]:8d}   {float(raw(d)):11.2f}   no")
    print("  => raw fitness diverges to infinity while the mathematics stands")
    print("     perfectly still: conservative inflation adds no semantic content.")

    # And the quantitative construction: exceed any prescribed target M.
    print()
    for M in (10, 1000, 10 ** 6):
        # Choose n > max(N, k) as in the proof, with c = 1/(2M):
        #   sqrt(n) <= n/(2M)  holds once n >= 4 M^2, and we need n > 2 M * len.
        n = max(4 * M * M, 2 * M * base[1]) + 1
        d = extend(base, n)
        assert raw(d) > M
        print(f"  target M = {M:>8}: inflate by n = {n:>14}"
              f"  -> raw fitness = {float(raw(d)):.2f} > {M}")
    print("  => no global champion exists on the unrestricted class; a champion")
    print("     is a meaningful notion only after resource normalisation.")

    print()
    print("  By contrast, on any FINITE normalised comparison class a champion")
    print("  always exists:")
    klass = [(12, 300), (9, 200), (25, 700), (4, 90)]
    best = max(klass, key=raw)
    for d in klass:
        mark = "  <-- champion" if d == best else ""
        print(f"    {d[0]:3d} statements / {d[1]:4d} lines"
              f"  = {float(raw(d)):.5f}{mark}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    demo_closure_minimality()
    demo_merge_accounting()
    demo_canonical_champion()
    demo_two_routes()
    demo_reuse_identity()
    demo_phase_transition()
    demo_candidate_counts()
    demo_adapter_valley()
    demo_metastability()
    demo_no_global_maximum()
    banner("All demonstrations completed; every assertion verified.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Measuring the Canonicity Gap: Heuristic versus Optimum under Alternative Proof Routes
demos.description: A randomised experiment isolating the exact point at which the theory stops being computable by a closure operation. With one chosen proof per statement, the canonical-closure heuristic — take the cheapest route for each statement and union them — is provably optimal, and the script confirms this on three hundred random instances (worst observed ratio exactly 1). It then increases the number of alternative routes per statement and compares the heuristic against an exact branch-and-bound minimum-cost cover, reporting the mean and worst cost ratio, the mean fraction of fitness lost (which equals one minus the reciprocal of the ratio, because fitness is the ordinal inverse of cost on a fixed corpus), and how often a gap opens at all. Two routes already open a gap on roughly three quarters of instances, costing on average around thirteen per cent of fitness, and the gap grows with the number of routes: choosing routes independently is blind to the material different statements could have shared. The script closes with the minimal obstruction itself — one statement, two unit-cost routes, equal fitness, empty intersection — showing that no least covering closure exists.
demos.code:
"""
Where the theory stops being easy: measuring the canonicity gap
===============================================================

With ONE chosen proof per statement, the cheapest library proving a corpus is
canonical: it is the transitive closure of the statements' proof bases, it is
contained in every self-contained development that proves the corpus, and it is
therefore the fitness champion outright.

The moment a statement admits TWO inequivalent proofs, that argument collapses.
Two cost-equal covering libraries can have empty intersection, so the covering
developments have no least element and no closure operation can find the
optimum.  What survives is existence: a minimum-cost cover is still attained.
The problem has quietly become a weighted set cover.

This experiment measures the damage.  Over random multi-route corpora we
compare:

  * the CANONICAL-CLOSURE HEURISTIC -- pick the individually cheapest route for
    each statement and take the union (exactly optimal when r = 1), against
  * the TRUE OPTIMUM -- an exact branch-and-bound minimum-cost cover.

and report the ratio, together with the resulting loss of fitness.  The
heuristic is blind to sharing between routes chosen for different statements,
which is precisely the effect that makes the optimisation hard.

Self-contained; run with `python3 demo2.py`.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from statistics import mean
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Set, Tuple

Item = int
Routes = Dict[int, List[Set[Item]]]


def cost_of(s: Set[Item], length: Callable[[Item], int]) -> int:
    return sum(length(i) for i in s)


def canonical_closure_heuristic(routes: Routes, length: Callable[[Item], int]) -> Set[Item]:
    """Cheapest single route per statement, unioned.  Exact when r = 1."""
    out: Set[Item] = set()
    for rs in routes.values():
        out |= min(rs, key=lambda r: cost_of(r, length))
    return out


def min_cost_cover(routes: Routes, length: Callable[[Item], int]) -> Tuple[FrozenSet[Item], int]:
    """Exact minimum-cost covering library, by branch and bound."""
    stmts = list(routes)
    best: Optional[FrozenSet[Item]] = None
    best_cost = [float("inf")]

    def rec(k: int, acc: Set[Item]) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        c = cost_of(acc, length)
        if c >= best_cost[0]:
            return
        if k == len(stmts):
            best, best_cost[0] = frozenset(acc), c
            return
        rs = routes[stmts[k]]
        if any(r <= acc for r in rs):
            rec(k + 1, acc)
            return
        for r in sorted(rs, key=lambda r: cost_of(r - acc, length)):
            rec(k + 1, acc | r)

    rec(0, set())
    assert best is not None
    return best, int(best_cost[0])


def random_instance(
    n_items: int, n_stmts: int, n_routes: int, route_size: int, rng: random.Random
) -> Tuple[Routes, Dict[Item, int]]:
    lengths = {i: rng.randint(1, 12) for i in range(n_items)}
    routes: Routes = {
        s: [set(rng.sample(range(n_items), route_size)) for _ in range(n_routes)]
        for s in range(n_stmts)
    }
    return routes, lengths


def single_route_check(rng: random.Random) -> None:
    """With one route per statement the heuristic is provably exact."""
    print("  Sanity check -- with a single route per statement the heuristic")
    print("  coincides with the optimum on every instance:")
    worst = 1.0
    for _ in range(300):
        routes, lengths = random_instance(10, 4, 1, 3, rng)
        length = lambda i: lengths[i]
        h = cost_of(canonical_closure_heuristic(routes, length), length)
        _, opt = min_cost_cover(routes, length)
        worst = max(worst, h / opt)
    print(f"    worst observed ratio over 300 instances: {worst:.4f}"
          f"  ({'exact' if worst == 1.0 else 'NOT exact'})")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__)
    rng = random.Random(20260806)

    single_route_check(rng)

    print()
    print("  Canonicity gap as the number of alternative routes grows")
    print("  (10 items, 5 corpus statements, routes of 3 items, 400 instances each)")
    print()
    print("   routes r | mean ratio | worst ratio | mean fitness lost | gap > 1")
    print("  " + "-" * 68)
    for r in (1, 2, 3, 4, 6):
        ratios: List[float] = []
        for _ in range(400):
            routes, lengths = random_instance(10, 5, r, 3, rng)
            length = lambda i: lengths[i]
            h = cost_of(canonical_closure_heuristic(routes, length), length)
            _, opt = min_cost_cover(routes, length)
            ratios.append(h / opt)
        # fitness is the ordinal inverse of cost on a fixed corpus, so the
        # fitness retained by the heuristic is exactly 1 / ratio.
        lost = mean(1 - 1 / x for x in ratios)
        frac = mean(1.0 if x > 1 + 1e-12 else 0.0 for x in ratios)
        print(f"   {r:8d} | {mean(ratios):10.4f} | {max(ratios):11.4f} |"
              f" {lost * 100:16.1f}% | {frac * 100:6.1f}%")
    print()
    print("  => at r = 1 the heuristic IS the theorem: ratio exactly 1.")
    print("     Every additional route opens a gap, because choosing routes")
    print("     independently ignores the material they could have shared.")

    print()
    print("  The minimal obstruction, exactly as in the theory:")
    length = lambda i: 1
    r1, r2 = {1}, {2}
    print(f"    one statement, routes {sorted(r1)} and {sorted(r2)},"
          f" both of cost {cost_of(r1, length)}")
    print(f"    fitness of each: {Fraction(1, cost_of(r1, length))}  (equal, hence both champions)")
    print(f"    intersection of the two closures: {sorted(r1 & r2)}  -- proves nothing")
    print("    => no least covering closure; the champion exists but is not canonical.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Canonical Transitive Dependency Closure and Dependency-Adjusted Cost
algorithms.description: The foundation of the whole cost model. Given a dependency structure and a set of directly used items, the algorithm computes the least dependency-closed superset of that base by worklist expansion: repeatedly adjoin the direct dependencies of everything already collected until nothing new appears. Termination is immediate in a finite universe because each round either adds an item or stops, and the result is canonical: it is dependency-closed, contains the base, and is contained in every dependency-closed set containing the base. This minimality is exactly what removes accounting slack from the cost model — no interested party can argue for a smaller bill. Summing the source length over the closure gives the dependency-adjusted cost, in which shared material is charged once however many times it is used. Because fitness on a fixed corpus is the ordinal inverse of cost, one closure computation per competitor suffices to identify the champion. Complexity: O(V + E) with a worklist, where V counts reachable items and E the dependency edges among them; space O(V).
algorithms.pseudocode:
FUNCTION TransitiveClosure(deps, base):
    S    <- copy of base
    work <- list of elements of base
    WHILE work is nonempty:
        i <- pop(work)
        FOR EACH j IN deps(i):
            IF j NOT IN S:
                S <- S union {j}
                push(work, j)
    RETURN S
    // postcondition: S is dependency-closed, base subset-of S,
    //                and S subset-of every dependency-closed T containing base

FUNCTION DependencyAdjustedCost(deps, base, length):
    RETURN sum of length(i) for i in TransitiveClosure(deps, base)

FUNCTION ChampionByCost(deps, competitors, length):
    // on a fixed corpus, maximal fitness = minimal dependency-adjusted cost
    RETURN argmin over c in competitors of
             DependencyAdjustedCost(deps, base(c), length)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: canonical transitive dependency closure and dependency-adjusted cost."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Set

Item = int
Deps = Dict[Item, Set[Item]]


def transitive_closure(deps: Deps, base: Iterable[Item]) -> Set[Item]:
    """Return the LEAST dependency-closed superset of `base`.

    A set S is dependency-closed when deps(i) is a subset of S for every i in S,
    i.e. when S is a self-contained development.  The set returned is closed,
    contains `base`, and is contained in every closed superset of `base`; this
    minimality is what makes the resulting cost model canonical.

    Complexity: O(V + E) with a worklist, where V is the number of reachable
    items and E the number of dependency edges among them.
    """
    out: Set[Item] = set(base)
    work: List[Item] = list(out)
    while work:
        i = work.pop()
        for j in deps.get(i, set()):
            if j not in out:
                out.add(j)
                work.append(j)
    return out


def dependency_adjusted_cost(
    deps: Deps, base: Iterable[Item], length: Callable[[Item], int]
) -> int:
    """Total source length of the transitive closure, each item charged once."""
    return sum(length(i) for i in transitive_closure(deps, base))


def is_dependency_closed(deps: Deps, s: Iterable[Item]) -> bool:
    sset = set(s)
    return all(deps.get(i, set()) <= sset for i in sset)


def champion_by_cost(
    deps: Deps,
    bases: Dict[str, Set[Item]],
    length: Callable[[Item], int],
) -> str:
    """Return the fitness champion among competitors proving the same corpus.

    On a fixed corpus, fitness (statements per unit cost) is the ordinal inverse
    of dependency-adjusted cost, so the champion is exactly the minimiser of
    cost.  One closure computation per competitor.
    """
    return min(bases, key=lambda k: dependency_adjusted_cost(deps, bases[k], length))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    deps: Deps = {0: set(), 1: {0}, 2: {1}, 3: {0}, 4: {3}, 5: set(), 6: {5}}
    length = lambda i: 5
    closure = transitive_closure(deps, {2, 4})
    print("closure of {2,4}:", sorted(closure))
    print("closed:", is_dependency_closed(deps, closure))
    print("cost:", dependency_adjusted_cost(deps, {2, 4}, length))
    print("champion:", champion_by_cost(
        deps, {"lean": {2}, "broad": {2, 4, 6}, "bloated": {2, 4, 6, 1}}, length))

algorithms.name: Composition Threshold Test: Shared Dependency Mass against Adapter Charge
algorithms.description: Decides in one measurement whether merging two developments raises or lowers fitness. Merging pools the two dependency closures, so material both depend on is charged once instead of twice, but it costs an adapter layer reconciling the two sets of conventions. Exact inclusion-exclusion gives composed cost plus shared mass equals duplicate cost plus adapter, so with a common corpus the entire comparison collapses to the sign of (shared mass minus adapter): below the threshold composition strictly increases fitness, at it composition is exactly neutral, above it composition strictly decreases fitness. The algorithm also returns the scale-free form of the same criterion — the adapter density and the dependency density, both obtained by dividing by the duplicate cost — so the test transfers unchanged between projects of different sizes, and the critical adapter charge itself, which is precisely the total source length of the shared material. Complexity: O(|C(T)| + |C(U)|) with hashed sets; the identity is asserted at run time as a self-check.
algorithms.pseudocode:
FUNCTION CompositionVerdict(C_T, C_U, adapter, corpus_size, length):
    cost_T   <- sum of length over C_T
    cost_U   <- sum of length over C_U
    pooled   <- sum of length over (C_T union C_U)
    shared   <- sum of length over (C_T intersect C_U)

    duplicate_cost <- cost_T + cost_U
    composed_cost  <- pooled + adapter
    ASSERT composed_cost + shared = duplicate_cost + adapter   // exact

    IF adapter < shared:  verdict <- "gain"      // fitness strictly increases
    ELSE IF adapter = shared: verdict <- "neutral"
    ELSE: verdict <- "loss"                      // fitness strictly decreases

    RETURN verdict,
           shared,
           dependency_density = shared  / duplicate_cost,
           adapter_density    = adapter / duplicate_cost,
           duplicated_fitness = corpus_size / duplicate_cost,
           composed_fitness   = corpus_size / composed_cost

FUNCTION CriticalAdapter(C_T, C_U, length):
    RETURN sum of length over (C_T intersect C_U)
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: composition threshold test (shared mass versus adapter charge)."""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, Set, Tuple

Item = int


def shared_mass(
    closure_t: Iterable[Item], closure_u: Iterable[Item], length: Callable[[Item], int]
) -> int:
    """Total source length of the material both developments depend on."""
    return sum(length(i) for i in set(closure_t) & set(closure_u))


def composition_verdict(
    closure_t: Set[Item],
    closure_u: Set[Item],
    adapter: int,
    n_corpus: int,
    length: Callable[[Item], int],
) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Decide whether merging two developments raises or lowers fitness.

    Merging pools the two dependency closures, so shared material is charged
    once instead of twice, but costs an adapter layer reconciling the two
    interfaces.  Exact inclusion-exclusion gives

        composed cost + shared mass = duplicate cost + adapter,

    so with a common corpus the fitness comparison is decided entirely by the
    sign of (shared mass - adapter):

        adapter <  shared mass  ->  composition strictly increases fitness
        adapter == shared mass  ->  composition is fitness neutral
        adapter >  shared mass  ->  composition strictly decreases fitness

    Complexity: O(|C(T)| + |C(U)|) with hashed sets.
    """
    cost_t = sum(length(i) for i in closure_t)
    cost_u = sum(length(i) for i in closure_u)
    pooled = sum(length(i) for i in closure_t | closure_u)
    shared = shared_mass(closure_t, closure_u, length)

    duplicate_cost = cost_t + cost_u
    composed_cost = pooled + adapter
    assert composed_cost + shared == duplicate_cost + adapter

    f_dup = Fraction(n_corpus, duplicate_cost)
    f_comp = Fraction(n_corpus, composed_cost)
    verdict = "gain" if adapter < shared else ("neutral" if adapter == shared else "loss")

    return {
        "shared_mass": shared,
        "duplicate_cost": duplicate_cost,
        "composed_cost": composed_cost,
        "dependency_density": Fraction(shared, duplicate_cost),
        "adapter_density": Fraction(adapter, duplicate_cost),
        "duplicated_fitness": f_dup,
        "composed_fitness": f_comp,
        "verdict": verdict,
    }


def critical_adapter(
    closure_t: Set[Item], closure_u: Set[Item], length: Callable[[Item], int]
) -> int:
    """The exact adapter charge at which the phase transition occurs."""
    return shared_mass(closure_t, closure_u, length)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    length = lambda i: 10
    ct, cu = {0, 1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4, 5}
    print("critical adapter:", critical_adapter(ct, cu, length))
    for a in (10, 20, 30):
        r = composition_verdict(ct, cu, a, 4, length)
        print(f"A={a:3d}  {r['duplicated_fitness']} -> {r['composed_fitness']}"
              f"   {r['verdict']}")

algorithms.name: Exact Enumeration of Usable Sub-Libraries via Component Decomposition
algorithms.description: Counts the dependency-closed subsets of a library — the pieces that can be torn off and read on their own — exactly. The algorithm exploits the exact multiplicativity theorem: if the items split into parts with no dependency crossing between them, the closed subsets of the whole are precisely the tuples of closed subsets of the parts (an explicit bijection, sending a closed set to its intersections with the parts and back by union). So the global count is the product over weakly connected components. Within a component, reachability makes the dependency relation a preorder and a closed subset is exactly a downward-closed set for it; these are enumerated by incremental insertion, each new item either staying out or entering together with everything it reaches. The count is exponential in the worst case and unavoidably so — a fully independent family of n items has 2^n closed subsets — but the enumeration is linear in the output size, and the two exact extremes 2^n (independent) and n+1 (chain) bracket every real library. The derived modularity index log2(N)/n places a library on the axis between monolith and fully modular, quantifying the trade-off in which dependencies enable reuse while destroying detachability.

algorithms.name: Minimum-Cost Covering Library under Alternative Proof Routes
algorithms.description: Solves the champion problem in the regime where the canonical construction fails. With one chosen proof per statement the cheapest covering library is the transitive closure of the proof bases, found by a closure computation. With alternative routes that is no longer possible: two cost-equal covering libraries can have empty intersection, so the covering developments have no least element and no closure operation can be exact. Existence nonetheless survives — a nonempty finite family of costs attains a minimum — so the algorithm searches for it by branch and bound, branching on statements in order, trying each route for the next statement not yet proved, skipping statements already proved for free by material bought earlier, and pruning against the incumbent. Ordering the branches by marginal rather than absolute route cost makes the pruning effective, because items already purchased are free thereafter. The worst case is exponential, as it must be: the problem is a weighted set cover in disguise. The module also supplies the canonical-closure heuristic (cheapest single route per statement, unioned), exact when there is one route and measurably suboptimal otherwise, together with the ratio between the two — the canonicity gap.
algorithms.pseudocode:
FUNCTION MinCostCover(routes, length):
    statements <- list of statements
    best      <- undefined
    best_cost <- +infinity

    PROCEDURE Search(k, acc):
        c <- sum of length over acc
        IF c >= best_cost: RETURN                    // prune
        IF k = |statements|:
            best <- acc ; best_cost <- c ; RETURN
        R <- routes(statements[k])
        IF some r IN R satisfies r subset-of acc:
            Search(k + 1, acc) ; RETURN              // already proved, free
        FOR EACH r IN R sorted by cost of (r minus acc) ascending:
            Search(k + 1, acc union r)

    Search(0, empty set)
    RETURN best, best_cost

FUNCTION CanonicalClosureHeuristic(routes, length):
    out <- empty set
    FOR EACH statement s:
        out <- out union (cheapest single route of s)
    RETURN out       // exactly optimal when every statement has one route

FUNCTION CanonicityGap(routes, length):
    RETURN cost(CanonicalClosureHeuristic(routes, length))
             / cost(MinCostCover(routes, length))
algorithms.code:
"""Algorithm: minimum-cost covering library under alternative proof routes."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, List, Optional, Set, Tuple

Item = int
Routes = Dict[str, List[Set[Item]]]


def canonical_closure_heuristic(
    routes: Routes, length: Callable[[Item], int]
) -> Set[Item]:
    """Greedy baseline: take the cheapest single route for each statement.

    With ONE route per statement this is exactly optimal -- the canonical
    library is the least covering closure.  With alternative routes the
    covering developments have no least element (two cost-equal covers can have
    empty intersection), so this heuristic can be strictly suboptimal: it
    ignores the sharing between routes chosen for different statements.
    Complexity: O(sum of route sizes).
    """
    out: Set[Item] = set()
    for rs in routes.values():
        out |= min(rs, key=lambda r: sum(length(i) for i in r))
    return out


def min_cost_cover(
    routes: Routes, length: Callable[[Item], int]
) -> Tuple[FrozenSet[Item], int]:
    """Exact minimum-cost covering library, by branch and bound.

    A collection proves a statement if it contains at least one of that
    statement's routes; it covers the corpus if it proves every statement.  A
    minimum-cost cover always exists (a nonempty finite family of naturals has
    a minimum), so the champion question stays well posed; it merely stops
    having a canonical answer.

    The search branches on statements in order, trying each route for the next
    uncovered statement and pruning against the incumbent.  Worst case is
    exponential -- the problem is a weighted set cover in disguise -- but the
    pruning is effective because already-purchased items are free thereafter.
    """
    stmts = list(routes)
    best: Optional[FrozenSet[Item]] = None
    best_cost = [float("inf")]

    def cost_of(s: Set[Item]) -> int:
        return sum(length(i) for i in s)

    def rec(k: int, acc: Set[Item]) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        c = cost_of(acc)
        if c >= best_cost[0]:
            return
        if k == len(stmts):
            best, best_cost[0] = frozenset(acc), c
            return
        rs = routes[stmts[k]]
        if any(r <= acc for r in rs):          # already proved for free
            rec(k + 1, acc)
            return
        # try cheapest marginal extension first, for better pruning
        for r in sorted(rs, key=lambda r: cost_of(r - acc)):
            rec(k + 1, acc | r)

    rec(0, set())
    assert best is not None
    return best, int(best_cost[0])


def canonicity_gap(routes: Routes, length: Callable[[Item], int]) -> float:
    """Ratio of the heuristic's cost to the true optimum (>= 1)."""
    h = canonical_closure_heuristic(routes, length)
    _, opt = min_cost_cover(routes, length)
    return sum(length(i) for i in h) / opt


if __name__ == "__main__":
    lengths = {1: 4, 2: 4, 3: 5, 4: 2, 5: 9}
    length = lambda i: lengths[i]
    routes: Routes = {
        "s1": [{1, 2}, {3}],
        "s2": [{2, 4}, {3, 4}],
        "s3": [{5}, {1, 3}],
    }
    cover, c = min_cost_cover(routes, length)
    h = canonical_closure_heuristic(routes, length)
    print("optimum  :", sorted(cover), "cost", c)
    print("heuristic:", sorted(h), "cost", sum(length(i) for i in h))
    print("gap      :", round(canonicity_gap(routes, length), 4))

visualizations.name: The Two Exact Accounting Laws: Composition Threshold and the Linear Reuse Saving
visualizations.description: Two panels showing the model's exact identities in action. The left panel plots the fitness of a composite as a function of the adapter charge against the flat fitness of keeping two developments separate; the curves cross exactly at the shared dependency mass, and the gain and loss regions are shaded on either side of that sharp critical point. The right panel plots the pooled cost of k specialists that each rebuild the same core against the cost of a shared library that writes the core once: the gap is exactly (k-1) copies of the core, marked at several values of k, which is why general libraries look like a bad deal for a single client and an obvious one for many.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the composition phase transition and the reuse saving.

Left panel  -- fitness of the composite as a function of the adapter charge A,
against the flat fitness of keeping the two developments separate.  The two
curves cross exactly at A = shared dependency mass; the crossing is the phase
transition, and it is sharp.

Right panel -- the exact k-fold reuse identity in action: the pooled cost of k
specialists that each rebuild the same core grows linearly with slope
cost(core), while the shared library that writes the core once stays flat plus
private material.  The vertical gap is exactly (k-1) * cost(core).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    # ---------------- left: phase transition ----------------
    n_corpus = 4
    duplicate_cost = 80.0      # closures {0,1,2,3} and {2,3,4,5}, all lengths 10
    pooled_cost = 60.0
    shared = duplicate_cost - pooled_cost      # = 20, the critical adapter

    A = np.linspace(0, 45, 400)
    composed = n_corpus / (pooled_cost + A)
    duplicated = np.full_like(A, n_corpus / duplicate_cost)

    ax1.plot(A, composed, lw=2.4, color="#1f77b4", label="compose (pool + adapter)")
    ax1.plot(A, duplicated, lw=2.4, ls="--", color="#d62728",
             label="keep separate (duplicate shared material)")
    ax1.axvline(shared, color="#444", lw=1.2, ls=":")
    ax1.fill_between(A, composed, duplicated, where=composed > duplicated,
                     color="#1f77b4", alpha=0.15)
    ax1.fill_between(A, composed, duplicated, where=composed < duplicated,
                     color="#d62728", alpha=0.15)
    ax1.annotate(f"critical adapter\nA = shared mass = {shared:.0f}",
                 xy=(shared, n_corpus / duplicate_cost),
                 xytext=(shared + 6, n_corpus / duplicate_cost + 0.012),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#444"), fontsize=10)
    ax1.text(4, 0.062, "COMPOSITION PAYS", color="#1f77b4", fontsize=11, weight="bold")
    ax1.text(28, 0.0425, "COMPOSITION COSTS", color="#d62728", fontsize=11, weight="bold")
    ax1.set_xlabel("adapter charge $A$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("fitness  (statements per unit cost)")
    ax1.set_title("Composition phase transition")
    ax1.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

    # ---------------- right: k-fold reuse ----------------
    core_cost = 12.0
    priv_cost = 6.0
    ks: List[int] = list(range(1, 13))
    suite = [k * (core_cost + priv_cost) for k in ks]
    library = [core_cost + k * priv_cost for k in ks]

    ax2.plot(ks, suite, "o-", lw=2.2, color="#d62728",
             label="suite of $k$ specialists (core rebuilt each time)")
    ax2.plot(ks, library, "s-", lw=2.2, color="#2ca02c",
             label="shared library (core written once)")
    for k in (4, 8, 12):
        ax2.annotate("", xy=(k, suite[k - 1]), xytext=(k, library[k - 1]),
                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#555", lw=1.1))
        ax2.text(k + 0.15, (suite[k - 1] + library[k - 1]) / 2,
                 f"$(k-1)\\cdot$core $= {int((k - 1) * core_cost)}$", fontsize=9)
    ax2.set_xlabel("number of client specialisations $k$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("dependency-adjusted cost")
    ax2.set_title("Exact reuse saving: $(k-1)$ wasted copies of the core")
    ax2.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.suptitle("Dependency-adjusted fitness: the two exact accounting laws",
                 fontsize=13, weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("phase_transition_and_reuse.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote phase_transition_and_reuse.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: The Shape of the Landscape: Adapter Valleys and Three-Style Metastability
visualizations.description: Two panels on the geometry of the landscape. The left panel draws a semantics-preserving migration between two developments written against inequivalent interfaces: the endpoints sit at (1+beta) times the intrinsic content, the boundary-crossing state at (1+alpha) times it, and the shaded band between them is the guaranteed relative overshoot (alpha-beta)/(1+beta), which no path can avoid however cleverly refactored. The right panel shows nine developments of one corpus, three per methodological style, with bounded refactorings connecting only same-style developments: each style contains its own strict local maximum, outlined in the plot, and only one of the three attains the global maximum — so no sequence of small local improvements leads from the algebraic peak to the strictly better combinatorial one.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: the shape of the fitness landscape.

Left panel  -- the adapter valley.  A semantics-preserving migration between
two developments written against inequivalent interfaces must pass through a
state that implements both, whose source length is at least (1+alpha) times the
intrinsic content while the endpoints sit at (1+beta) times it.  The guaranteed
relative overshoot (alpha-beta)/(1+beta) is drawn as a shaded floor: no path,
however clever, can stay below it.

Right panel -- three-style metastability.  Nine developments of one corpus,
three per methodological style, with bounded refactorings connecting only
same-style developments.  Each style contains its own strict local maximum;
only one of the three is global, so no sequence of small local improvements
leads from one peak to a better one.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    # ---------------- left: adapter valley ----------------
    content = 100.0
    alpha, beta = 0.5, 0.1
    endpoint = (1 + beta) * content          # 110
    crossing = (1 + alpha) * content         # 150
    floor = endpoint * (1 + (alpha - beta) / (1 + beta))

    steps = np.arange(7)
    path = np.array([endpoint, 118, 132, crossing, 134, 119, endpoint])

    ax1.plot(steps, path, "o-", lw=2.4, color="#8e44ad", label="a migration path")
    ax1.axhline(endpoint, color="#2ca02c", ls="--", lw=1.6,
                label=r"endpoint length $(1+\beta)C = 110$")
    ax1.axhline(floor, color="#d62728", ls=":", lw=1.8,
                label=r"guaranteed peak $(1+\alpha)C = 150$")
    ax1.fill_between([-0.3, 6.3], endpoint, floor, color="#d62728", alpha=0.10)
    ax1.annotate(
        r"every path must reach here:" "\n"
        r"overshoot $\geq \frac{\alpha-\beta}{1+\beta} = \frac{4}{11} \approx 36\%$",
        xy=(3, crossing), xytext=(3.4, 141),
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#444"), fontsize=10)
    ax1.scatter([3], [crossing], s=140, facecolor="none", edgecolor="#d62728", lw=2.2,
                zorder=5)
    ax1.text(0.05, 106, "interface A", fontsize=9, color="#2ca02c")
    ax1.text(5.2, 106, "interface B", fontsize=9, color="#2ca02c")
    ax1.set_xlim(-0.3, 6.3)
    ax1.set_xlabel("step along the migration")
    ax1.set_ylabel("source length")
    ax1.set_title("The adapter valley is unavoidable")
    ax1.legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=9)
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25)

    # ---------------- right: three-style metastability ----------------
    fit = [1, 2, 5, 3, 7, 4, 6, 2, 9]
    styles = ["algebraic"] * 3 + ["analytic"] * 3 + ["combinatorial"] * 3
    colors = ["#1f77b4"] * 3 + ["#ff7f0e"] * 3 + ["#2ca02c"] * 3
    peaks = {2, 4, 8}

    xs = np.arange(9)
    bars = ax2.bar(xs, fit, color=colors, alpha=0.85,
                   edgecolor=["black" if i in peaks else "none" for i in range(9)],
                   linewidth=[2.2 if i in peaks else 0 for i in range(9)])
    for i in peaks:
        ax2.text(i, fit[i] + 0.25, "local\nmax", ha="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold")
    for start, label in ((0, "algebraic"), (3, "analytic"), (6, "combinatorial")):
        ax2.axvspan(start - 0.5, start + 2.5, color=colors[start], alpha=0.07)
        ax2.text(start + 1, -1.05, label, ha="center", fontsize=10)
    ax2.axhline(9, color="#2ca02c", ls=":", lw=1.5)
    ax2.text(0.1, 9.15, "global maximum", fontsize=9, color="#2ca02c")
    ax2.set_ylim(-1.6, 10.6)
    ax2.set_xticks(xs)
    ax2.set_xlabel("development (bounded refactorings stay within a style)")
    ax2.set_ylabel("fitness")
    ax2.set_title("Three styles, three peaks, one summit")
    ax2.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)

    fig.suptitle("The shape of the landscape: valleys between peaks",
                 fontsize=13, weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("valley_and_metastability.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote valley_and_metastability.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.name: Between n+1 and 2^n: How Dependency Density Collapses the Candidate Population
visualizations.description: The exact trade-off behind reuse, plotted. The left panel shows on a logarithmic scale the two exact extremes — an independent family of n items admits exactly 2^n usable sub-libraries, a chain exactly n+1 — with randomly generated dependency structures of increasing edge density interpolating between them; every real library lives inside the shaded region. The right panel plots the modularity index log2(N)/n against edge density at fixed n, showing the smooth collapse from fully modular (index 1) towards monolithic as dependencies accumulate: exactly the mechanism that makes a core shareable is what makes its fragments undetachable.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: how dependency density collapses the population of usable
sub-libraries.

A usable sub-library is a dependency-closed subset: one that can be extracted
and read on its own.  A fully independent family of n items has exactly 2^n of
them; a chain, in which each item depends on the previous one, has exactly
n + 1.  Every real library lives between these two exact extremes, and where it
lives is a measurable structural invariant.

The left panel plots the two exact extremes on a logarithmic scale together
with randomly sampled dependency structures of increasing edge density.  The
right panel shows the modularity index log2(count)/n, which is 1 for a fully
modular library and tends to 0 for a monolith.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from typing import Dict, List, Set

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def count_closed_subsets(deps: Dict[int, Set[int]], n: int) -> int:
    """Count dependency-closed subsets by incremental ideal construction."""
    reach: Dict[int, Set[int]] = {}
    for i in range(n):
        seen, stack = {i}, [i]
        while stack:
            x = stack.pop()
            for y in deps.get(x, set()):
                if y not in seen:
                    seen.add(y)
                    stack.append(y)
        reach[i] = seen
    ideals: Set[frozenset] = {frozenset()}
    for i in range(n):
        ideals = {s for t in ideals for s in (t, frozenset(t | reach[i]))}
    return len(ideals)


def random_dag(n: int, p: float, rng: random.Random) -> Dict[int, Set[int]]:
    """Random acyclic dependency structure: item i may depend on items j < i."""
    return {i: {j for j in range(i) if rng.random() < p} for i in range(n)}


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(20260806)
    ns = list(range(1, 15))
    free = [2 ** n for n in ns]
    chain = [n + 1 for n in ns]

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

    ax1.semilogy(ns, free, "o-", lw=2.4, color="#2ca02c",
                 label=r"independent family: exactly $2^n$")
    ax1.semilogy(ns, chain, "s-", lw=2.4, color="#d62728",
                 label=r"chain: exactly $n+1$")
    for p, colour in ((0.10, "#1f77b4"), (0.30, "#9467bd"), (0.60, "#8c564b")):
        vals = []
        for n in ns:
            trials = [count_closed_subsets(random_dag(n, p, rng), n) for _ in range(12)]
            vals.append(float(np.exp(np.mean(np.log(trials)))))
        ax1.semilogy(ns, vals, "--", lw=1.8, color=colour,
                     label=f"random structure, edge density $p={p}$")
    ax1.fill_between(ns, chain, free, color="grey", alpha=0.08)
    ax1.set_xlabel("number of items $n$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("usable sub-libraries (log scale)")
    ax1.set_title("Dependency density collapses the candidate population")
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.25, which="both")

    # modularity index
    ps = np.linspace(0, 1, 21)
    n = 12
    idx = []
    for p in ps:
        trials = [count_closed_subsets(random_dag(n, float(p), rng), n) for _ in range(20)]
        idx.append(float(np.mean([np.log2(t) / n for t in trials])))
    ax2.plot(ps, idx, "o-", lw=2.4, color="#1f77b4")
    ax2.axhline(1.0, color="#2ca02c", ls="--", lw=1.6, label="fully modular ($2^n$)")
    ax2.axhline(np.log2(n + 1) / n, color="#d62728", ls=":", lw=1.8,
                label=r"monolith ($n+1$)")
    ax2.set_ylim(0, 1.08)
    ax2.set_xlabel("dependency edge density $p$")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"modularity index  $\log_2 N / n$")
    ax2.set_title(f"Reuse versus modularity ($n = {n}$)")
    ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.25)

    fig.suptitle("Between $n+1$ and $2^n$: the exact trade-off behind reuse",
                 fontsize=13, weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("candidate_counts.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote candidate_counts.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
